findings.source_quote: αὐτοὶ αὐτὰ φυγαδεύοντες καὶ ἱκετευόμενοι ὑπ’ αὐτῶν
findings.english_quote: The neuter αὐτά can collect both the demons and the demonic sufferings just mentioned, whereas the masculine αὐτῶν most naturally refers specifically to the demons.
findings.issue: The note misleadingly contrasts αὐτά with a supposedly gender-distinguishing αὐτῶν. The genitive plural αὐτῶν has the same form in all genders. Taking its referent as the demons is contextually defensible, especially because they can implore the hearers, but the inflection does not establish that referent. The main English pronouns remain defensible.
findings.suggested_revision: Revise the note to explain that αὐτά may refer to the sufferings or collectively to the preceding demons and sufferings, while αὐτῶν is formally compatible with any gender. Identify supplication, rather than morphological gender, as the reason for preferring demons as the latter pronoun’s referent. Preserve the alternative reference and submit the revised note for fresh review.

findings.source_quote: ἡ τοῦ θεοῦ χεὶρ εἰς ἴασιν αὐτοῦ ἐπιψαῦσαι δυνηθῇ ὡς ἁγνοῦ καὶ πιστεύοντος
findings.english_quote: Although the pronoun follows a reference to the body, the masculine participles ἁγνοῦ and πιστεύοντος identify the referent as the afflicted person.
findings.issue: ἁγνοῦ is an adjective, not a participle. Both ἁγνοῦ and πιστεύοντος have forms shared by masculine and neuter genitive singulars, so morphology alone does not distinguish the afflicted person from a metonymic reference to the body. The personal referent is defensible from context, especially the attribution of believing, but the note overstates its grammatical certainty. The preceding assertion that αὐτοῦ belongs to ἐπιψαῦσαι also leaves undisclosed its possible attachment to ἴασιν.
findings.suggested_revision: Correct the grammatical description: ἁγνοῦ is an adjective and πιστεύοντος a participle, and both forms permit masculine or neuter agreement. Explain that the main rendering chooses the afflicted person on contextual and semantic grounds, while a metonymic reference to the body remains possible. Also acknowledge αὐτοῦ with ἴασιν ('for his healing') as an alternative to construing it with ἐπιψαῦσαι ('touch him'). The main wording need not change solely because of these alternatives; the revised disclosure requires fresh review.
